# Recipes — tool import and chain examples

The recipes follow the cookbook grammar. *Problem* names the operational
need. *Solution* is the exact command to run. *Discussion* explains the
mechanics behind it. Every `Solution` in this page ran. Its `Observation`
carries the captured output of that run. Nothing here is aspirational.
`pqscan` reads upstream output as input lines. It needs no extra flag
unless the format needs disambiguation.

``` {mermaid}

```

## Input chains

### Domain discovery → cipher truth

**Problem.** List the live subdomains of a zone. Then read the
key-exchange group and the cipher suite the TLS stack actually negotiates
against a modern client. The wire answers — the administrator's
configuration does not.

**Solution.**

```bash
subfinder -d shain.io -silent \
  | httpx -silent -no-color \
  | pqscan -jsonl -o assets.jsonl
```

**Observation.** One schema-1 record per endpoint. This run's chain found
4 alive endpoints. The first record carries the tools' stamps at capture
time: subfinder v2.16.0 → httpx v1.12.0:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"oi.shain.io","host":"oi.shain.io","ip":"","port":443,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":false,"state":"skipped: no alt-svc h3 hint","negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":false,"h3_direct":false}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"sha256WithRSAEncryption","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"RSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false,"summary":"negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40)"},"error":""}
```

**Discussion.** subfinder streams bare domains. httpx resolves the domains
and probes them. It answers `scheme://host` lines. The input grammar strips
those lines to host specs natively. The chain needs no flag and no adapter.
The probe is browser-grade. The ClientHello offers the stdlib default
group preference order (MLKEM hybrid first). It offers ALPN `h2,http/1.1`.
It records what the server SELECTED. Negotiation is the assertion. No
configuration parsing. Each upstream tool keeps its own job. Nothing in the
chain re-implements another tool's job. The text chain needs only the
tools. A httpx `-csv` render refuses at import — the documented boundary.
The text dialect is the whole import contract.

### Port truth first

**Problem.** Only hosts that actually accept on a given port need a probe
handshake. A closed socket wastes the retry budget. It skews the latency
numbers.

**Solution.**

```bash
naabu -l domains.txt -p 443,8443,465,993 -silent \
  | pqscan -jsonl
```

**Observation.** naabu's `host:port` lines are first-class target specs.
One probe handshake and one record go out per surviving socket (naabu
2.6.1 at capture time).

**Discussion.** naabu is the port-discovery plane. It answers with the
sockets that accept. That answer is the input pqscan wants. The
certificate-directory collection and the resumption analysis reuse these
records later. They do not re-dial. `-from-naabu` also covers naabu's
bare-host-and-ports-block rendering. The `host:port` form above is already
first-class. A saved render also scans through the flag form (the next
recipe).

### Import dialects render as files — -from-httpx / -from-naabu / -from-nuclei

**Problem.** The import tools carry three render dialects. httpx answers
scheme-URI lines (`https://host:port`, plus an optional URL path suffix).
naabu answers `host:port` lines. It also renders a host line followed by
its bare-port block. `nuclei -j` streams findings JSONL (one JSON finding
per line; its `matched-at` field carries the probed host). The render may
already sit on disk. The operator reads that file without a cleanup pass:
the adapters accept the render the way any target file is accepted.

**Solution.**

```bash
cat domains.txt | httpx -silent -ports 443,8443 -p 443,8443 -no-color > discovered.httpx   # the pinned capture (httpx v1.12.0)
pqscan -from-httpx discovered.httpx -jsonl

naabu -l domains.txt -p 443,8443,465,993 -silent > naabu.naabu   # the pinned capture (naabu 2.6.1)
pqscan -from-naabu naabu.naabu -jsonl

nuclei -l hosts.txt -silent -j > nuclei.jsonl   # the pinned capture (nuclei v3.11.1)
pqscan -from-nuclei nuclei.jsonl -jsonl
```

**Observation.** The imports ran with the real tools. Each import read its
pinned capture of that exact command. The upstream renders stay verbatim.
The records come from the pqscan legs. The httpx render's scheme/URI lines
strip to host:port specs:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"example.org","host":"example.org","ip":"","port":443,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":true,"state":"negotiated","negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":true,"h3_direct":true}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"ecdsa-with-SHA256","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"ECDSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false,"summary":"negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40)"},"error":""}
```

and the naabu render's doubled `host:port` lines (`example.com:8443`,
`example.com:443` twice over — naabu renders per resolved address).
They dedupe to one record per socket:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"example.com:8443","host":"example.com","ip":"","port":8443,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":false,"state":"skipped: no alt-svc h3 hint","negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":false,"h3_direct":false}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"ecdsa-with-SHA256","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"ECDSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false,"summary":"negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40)"},"error":""}
```

the import: the pinned capture (nuclei v3.11.1, `hosts.txt =
scanme.sh`, the default template set) answers 28 findings on stdout. The
import reads the file. The one dedupe step collapses the repeated sockets
to two records — the ssh port's record (a real error record:
the TCP plane reached an ssh service) and the https port's record:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"scanme.sh:22","host":"scanme.sh","ip":"","port":22,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","suite":"","version":"","alpn_neg":""},"quic":{"attempted":false,"state":"","negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":false,"h3_direct":false}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":0,"label":"","hndl":false,"summary":""},"error":"tls: first record does not look like a TLS handshake"}
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"scanme.sh:443","host":"scanme.sh","ip":"","port":443,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":29,"group_name":"x25519","group_class":"classic","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":false,"state":"skipped: no alt-svc h3 hint","negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":false,"h3_direct":false}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"ecdsa-with-SHA256","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"ECDSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":0,"label":"scan-error","hndl":false,"summary":"weak_classical_preferred(-5)"},"error":""}
```

**Discussion.** The adapters feed the SAME composition the
`-u`/`-l`/`--` parse path uses. `internal/target` strips the dialect
decoration. Every line goes through the one grammar. One dedupe step
serves every input source in flag order. The key is host:port; first
occurrence wins. A bad line refuses the run named by its flag (exit 64).
The run never scans a truncated list. The httpx `-csv` direction is out
of contract by decision. The pinned text command is the whole httpx
import. The block rendering of a naabu multi-port run parses through
`-from-naabu` exactly as the host:port lines do. The block is a host line
followed by bare-decimal port lines (the adapter's unit fixtures pin it).
The `-from-*` adapters read files. The findings arrive on stdout of the
pinned `nuclei -j` capture. The recipe writes them to the file the
import reads. A `-from-nuclei -` value reads as a file name
(`open -: no such file or directory`, exit 64). `nuclei ... -j` writes
JSONL to stdout. `> findings.jsonl` puts it on disk.

### Internet scale — one box of a four-box pass

**Problem.** A /16-class target list needs a TLS sweep in one pass. The
run must stay off a 16-hour serial tail. One box's failure must not orphan
the run's output.

**Solution.**

```bash
masscan -p 443 -iL cidrs.txt --rate=100000 --open-only -oX - \
  | pqscan -jsonl -o shard1.jsonl
```

**Observation.** masscan answers the port question at line rate. pqscan
answers the cipher-configuration question per surviving socket. One
schema-1 record stream leaves the other side.

**Discussion.** The two tools compose because their contracts are
narrow. masscan's `-oX -` and `--open-only` keep the pipe to the sockets
that accept. pqscan adds the negotiated group, suite, ALPN, QUIC and
certificate blocks per host. The shard split is the flag's job now:
`-shard i/n` filters the composed targets to one box's slice. The rule:
`fnv1a64(host:port) % n == i-1`. The shards stay disjoint and complete
at a fixed total. The four boxes run the same list. Each box runs its own
`-shard 1/4 … 4/4`. The union of the four record streams is the run. The
stderr note carries the slice's count (`shard 1/4: N of M targets`).
Each box bounds its own handshake budget with `-rate`/`-threads`. A
re-run replays the WAL. It does not re-dial the surviving targets. Live
partition proof on a 9-target list; both slice notes:

```text
pqscan: shard 1/2: 4 of 9 targets
pqscan: shard 2/2: 5 of 9 targets
```

### Target grammar and its refusals

**Problem.** The input contract is exact. The contract names what pqscan
accepts. It names what pqscan refuses. A scanner fails closed on the
malformed target specs. It never mis-scans.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u example.com:8443 -jsonl      # host:port
pqscan -u 2001:db8::1 -jsonl           # v6 literal
echo http://example.org:8443 | pqscan -jsonl -   # scheme:// strips on the stdin alias
echo 'https://example.org:443/api' | pqscan -jsonl   # refused: a URL path suffix
printf '198.51.100.0/24\n' | pqscan -jsonl           # refused: CIDR spec
```

**Observation.** The first three run. The scheme strips off every spec
line (`-u`, `-l` lines, the piped stdin). One schema-1 record goes out
per target. `example.com:8443` negotiates. The unreachable v6 literal is
a record with `error` set. It is not a refusal:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"example.com:8443","host":"example.com","ip":"","port":8443,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":false,"state":"skipped: no alt-svc h3 hint","negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":false,"h3_direct":false}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"ecdsa-with-SHA256","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"ECDSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false,"summary":"negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40)"},"error":""}
```

What refuses (exit 64, nothing scanned): a URL path suffix on the spec
path (path stripping stays the adapters' job). A CIDR spec line also
refuses (per-address expansion is planned):

```text
pqscan: URL path "/api" in target spec "https://example.org:443/api": a URL path is the -from-httpx adapter's decoration (-from-httpx FILE strips scheme and path; the spec path keeps host[:port])
```

```text
pqscan: -cidr target "198.51.100.0/24": cidr expansion is not supported
```

**Discussion.** The grammar takes these forms. Bare hosts (443 default).
`host:port`. IPv4/IPv6 literals (bracketed v6 with port).
`scheme://host[:port]` (the scheme strips on every spec line). `i/n`
shard specs. The stdin forms below.
The pipe is the implicit default input (no marker needed). `-l -` is the
explicit stdin-file alias. `--` composes beside `-u`/`-l`. Every flag
also parses under two dashes (`--mode` is `-mode`). The completions offer
both spellings. Specs dedupe by host:port in input order. Unreachable
endpoints are NOT refusals. They are records with `error` set. The
failure-taxonomy recipe below classifies them. CIDR spec lines refuse.
Per-address expansion is not supported (the grammar parses the class;
the expansion is the boundary).

## Modes: fast, deep, pq

### Deep standard — the bounded ≤24-probe profile

**Problem.** Beyond the one fast handshake: the per-rung answers for
every named group. The QUIC plane's answers for the same rungs, for the
RFC 9369 transport version, and for one completed HTTP/3 exchange. The
ML-DSA signature offer set. The HRR demand. Deep standard reads these
out without the full matrix's cost on every asset.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -jsonl
```

**Observation.** The record gains a `deep` block. This run's counts and
a finding excerpt (the 24th finding is the HRR row):

```text
mode=standard attempted=24 ok=3 rejected=9
group/4585    rejected   alert 40
group/4586    rejected   alert 40
group/4587    rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/4589    rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/4590    rejected   alert 40
group/25      rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/29      accepted   negotiated x25519, suite TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, tls-1.3
quic/v2       rejected   no compatible QUIC version found (we support [v2], server offered [0x4a6a1afa v1 draft-29])
quic/h3-exchange accepted h3 exchange completed: status 301 (GET /, alpn h3, quic-v1)
sigalg/mldsa65 refused    not-offerable: the raw ClientHello path pins its signature_algorithms list (custom-list offers are not offered)
hrr/x25519-shareless  accepted   hrr: the server requested group x25519 (29)
```

with the text line carrying the counts tail `deep=standard:24p/3ok/9rej`.
The remaining 12 of the 24 findings are the `refused` rows: three
classical groups the stdlib cannot offer, three QUIC rungs, three
ML-DSA sigalgs, three resumption vectors. Each row is its own finding.

**Discussion.** The profile handshake runs first. Its facts prune the
plan. The plan never re-probes the negotiated group. It never re-probes
the negotiated (suite, version) pair. It never re-probes the negotiated
version. It never re-probes the certificate probe. It never re-probes
the QUIC rung the profile already answered. The plan then cuts to the ≤24 budget
through the documented prune classes. The classes run in order. Adjacent
suites first. Then suites on the observed version. Then the remaining
suites. Then the foreign-version probes. Then the classic signature
algorithms. The prune classes never touch: the forced-group offer set. The ML-DSA
sigalgs. The cert probe. The 0-RTT probe. The HRR probe. On a
modern host (the live reference above) the plan keeps exactly the
structural offer sets: the group offer set, the QUIC offer set, the
sigalg offer set, resumption, HRR. The legacy suite and version hunt
lives in `-deep full`. Per-kind dispatch: a group probe offers ONE named
group. The offer is a real share where the toolchain holds one. Where
the toolchain holds none, the probe sends a share-less raw offer (the
obsolete-Kyber oracle). `refused` rows are locally not-offerable probes.
The raw ClientHello path pins its signature_algorithms list. The
resumption plane is not instrumented yet. The finding's detail says
exactly that. A `refused` row is a capability boundary. It is not a
server answer. The HRR probe extracts the group the server DEMANDED
when the client withheld a share. The v2 rung offers the RFC 9369
transport version alone. A version-negotiation miss maps the server's
answer to a rejected row, verbatim. A v2 negotiation maps the accepted
row with the quic-v2 tail. The h3-exchange rung reads the server's
SETTINGS frame after the v1 handshake and runs one HTTP/3 GET. A
completed exchange maps the accepted row with the status. A negotiated
handshake that completes no exchange maps its own rejected row.

### Deep full — the complete offer-one matrix

**Problem.** Deep full gives exhaustive coverage: every suite × version
pair (the secure default list AND the legacy/insecure suites). Every
registry group. The signature-algorithm surface. The resumption vectors.
The QUIC plane's rungs. The HRR hop. Each row is one handshake.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -deep full -jsonl
```

**Observation.** (live) The record's `deep` block counts:

```json
{"mode":"full","attempted":82,"ok":29,"rejected":34}
```

(The remaining 19 findings are the `refused` rows.) Sample suite
findings (the legacy hunt lives here):

```text
suite/TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA@1.0   accepted   negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.0
suite/TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA@1.2   accepted   negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.2
suite/TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256@1.3           refused    not-offerable on tls-1.3: crypto/tls offers the fixed 1.3 suite set (offer-one is not client-restrictable)
suite/TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA@1.2     rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
```

The QUIC plane's rungs ride the same list. The v2 rung answers the
version-negotiation miss here as a rejected row, verbatim:

```text
quic/v2            rejected   no compatible QUIC version found (we support [v2], server offered [v1 0xeaba1aba draft-29])
quic/h3-exchange   accepted   h3 exchange completed: status 301 (GET /, alpn h3, quic-v1)
```

**Discussion.** 82 probes run. Observed facts prune none: 4 versions,
11 registry groups (4585–4590 plus the classical set), 47 suite×version
pairs, 7 signature algorithms (incl. the ML-DSA codepoints), 1
certificate, 3 resumption vectors, 1 HRR, plus the 8 QUIC-plane rungs.
The 8 QUIC rungs carry: the 6 group rungs, the RFC 9369
transport-version rung, the functional HTTP/3 rung.
The list auto-tracks `crypto/tls`. A Go upgrade that gains a suite
grows the matrix. Standard never exceeds its 24-probe budget. `full`
trades the budget for coverage. Point it at ONE asset. It is not the
run for a target list.

### -mode pq — the PQ offer set

**Problem.** Which post-quantum groups does this server accept rung by
rung — independent of the client's default preference order. Does it
still negotiate an obsolete draft.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode pq -jsonl
```

**Observation.** (live) The record's handshake block carries the offer
set's first ACCEPTED hybrid. The offer set lands as a deep-mode-shaped
block: `mode:"pq"` with the counts `8 attempted / 1 ok / 7 rejected`
and one finding per rung. The `-text` line rides the same counts as the
tail `deep=pq:8p/1ok/7rej`:

```text
group/4588   accepted    negotiated X25519MLKEM768, suite TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, tls-1.3
group/4590   rejected    alert 40
group/25497  rejected    alert 40
group/25498  rejected    alert 40
```

under `-explain` the reading names the accepted rung and the refusals
in operator words:

```text
  - deep: the forced PQ offer set sent 8 offers: 1 accepted, 7 refused with the server's reasons, 0 not-offerable; accepted: group/4588; each forced PQ-only group refused unless the server supports that group — the per-probe detail lives in the jsonl findings.
```

**Discussion.** `-mode pq` runs the PQ offer set: 4585–4590 plus the
Kyber drafts (25497/25498). The readiness rating rides the record's `pq`
block. A draft-HRR acceptance trips `pq.hndl` — the
harvest-now-decrypt-later flag. Material intercepted against a
draft-group handshake decrypts when the draft breaks. The rest of the
suite may look modern. The obsolete-Kyber oracle is the share-less offer
of 25497. The HRR answers by demanding the draft. That finding feeds the
compat decisions. Schedule this mode FIRST on any asset whose
`pq.label` reads below `pq-ready-hybrid`.

## The cipher questions

### Which ciphers does the server accept?

**Problem.** For a given host: does the stack support a specific cipher
suite? Or does it refuse one? Is ChaCha20-Poly1305 in the modern set? Is
the legacy CBC family still open on TLS 1.0–1.2? The wire answers each
question with one handshake.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -deep full -jsonl \
  | jq -r '.deep.findings[] | select(.probe | startswith("suite/")) | "\(.probe)\t\(.result)\t\(.detail)"'
```

**Observation.** (live, excerpt)

```text
suite/TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256@1.3            refused   not-offerable on tls-1.3: crypto/tls offers the fixed 1.3 suite set (offer-one is not client-restrictable)
suite/TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256@1.3      refused   not-offerable on tls-1.3: crypto/tls offers the fixed 1.3 suite set (offer-one is not client-restrictable)
suite/TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA@1.0   accepted   negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.0
suite/TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA@1.2   accepted   negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.2
```

**Discussion.** Each suite probe is its OWN handshake: it offers ONE
suite (offer-one / observe-accept). No shared negotiation sits behind
the row. An `accepted` row is unambiguous. TLS 1.0–1.2 suites are
individually forceable. TLS 1.3's ciphers ride one fixed set.
`crypto/tls` cannot restrict it. Those rows read `refused` with the
reason in the detail. The 1.3 SET acceptance still shows in the record's
`handshake.suite`. The profile handshake sets that field. The
`-probe-suite` override (planned) offers suites not in the registry
list. Until it lands, the matrix covers the stdlib lists. Those lists
auto-track per Go release.

### Which TLS versions does the server still accept?

**Problem.** The legacy-version floor is the standard audit question:
is TLS 1.0/1.1 still open? Which legacy stacks still serve?

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -deep full -jsonl \
  | jq -r '.deep.findings[] | select(.probe | startswith("version/")) | "\(.probe)\t\(.result): \(.detail)"'
```

**Observation.** (live)

```text
version/1.0    accepted: negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.0
version/1.1    accepted: negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.1
version/1.2    accepted: negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, tls-1.2
version/1.3    accepted: negotiated TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, tls-1.3
```

**Discussion.** The version hunt runs in the `full` matrix. When the
budget gets tight, the standard plan's prune classes drop the
foreign-version probes. (The live reference's standard run planned none:
the offer sets already filled the 24-probe budget.) Pair the version
rows with the suite rows. The 1.0/1.1 answers negotiated an
ECDSA-keyed CBC suite. A legacy-only answer. The fast plane never shows
it: the browser-grade handshake always lands 1.3. The deep modes exist
for this reason. The fast record reads "modern and hybrid". The deep
findings add "and still answering on a decade-old CBC stack".

### Which PQ groups does the server accept when probed?

**Problem.** Not negotiation-by-default: forced acceptability. Which of
the ML-KEM hybrids (4585–4590) and the legacy drafts does this server
take? What alert answers each refusal?

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -jsonl \
  | jq -r '.deep.findings[] | select(.probe | startswith("group/")) | "\(.probe)\t\(.result)\t\(.detail)"'
```

**Observation.** (live)

```text
group/4585    rejected   alert 40
group/4586    rejected   alert 40
group/4587    rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/4589    rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/4590    rejected   alert 40
group/25      rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/26      refused    not-offerable locally: tls: no supported key exchange methods (CurveIDs)
group/27      refused    not-offerable locally: tls: no supported key exchange methods (CurveIDs)
group/28      refused    not-offerable locally: tls: no supported key exchange methods (CurveIDs)
group/29      accepted   negotiated x25519, suite TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, tls-1.3
```

**Discussion.** `rejected` rows carry the server's own alert. Alert 40
is the group refused at the ClientHello. The `tls: handshake failure`
form is the server's stricter mid-handshake reply. Either way the
server ANSWERED and said no. That is a finding, not a failure.
`refused` rows are the honest tool boundary: no stdlib share exists for
that codepoint yet. The HRR finding closes the set. The client
withholds everything. The server DEMANDS a group in its
HelloRetryRequest. That demand is the last acceptability datum.

### Which signature algorithms are offered / possible?

**Problem.** PQ certificate signatures (ML-DSA/SLH-DSA) on the wire:
what is provable today? Where is the boundary?

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -jsonl \
  | jq -r '.deep.findings[] | select(.probe | startswith("sigalg/")) | "\(.probe)\t\(.result)\t\(.detail)"'
```

**Observation.** (live; every sigalg row refuses with its reason)

```text
sigalg/mldsa44   refused   not-offerable: the raw ClientHello path pins its signature_algorithms list (custom-list offers are not offered)
sigalg/mldsa65   refused   not-offerable: the raw ClientHello path pins its signature_algorithms list (custom-list offers are not offered)
sigalg/mldsa87   refused   not-offerable: the raw ClientHello path pins its signature_algorithms list (custom-list offers are not offered)
```

**Discussion.** The certificate analytics are provable today. They ride
the record's `cert` block: the leaf chain's signature algorithm
(`ecdsa-with-SHA256`), the key algorithm, the PQ-ness, the dual-cert
rule. `cert.dual` goes true when a classical-signed and a PQ-signed
member coexist in the offered chain. Custom signature_algorithms offers
in the raw ClientHello are the planned surface. Until then, the sigalg
probe rows state the boundary per finding. They never vanish. The
`-probe-sigalgs` override (planned) offers arbitrary lists.

## Debugging and fault logging

### Logging a fault: -debug and the live stream

**Problem.** A run can misbehave. The operator then needs the full
decision trail: human-readable and live.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u 127.0.0.1:64444 -debug
```

**Observation.** (live, stderr + the record on stdout)

```text
  21:43:45.775 [info][config] run : diagnostics armed  positional_args= version=0.0.1
  21:43:45.775 [info][engine] pipeline : multi-target scan started  max_window=1 progress_every=50 rate=0 total=1
  21:43:45.776 [error][tls] scan 127.0.0.1: TCP probe refused (dial tcp 127.0.0.1:64444: connect: connection refused)
  21:43:45.776 [info][engine] pipeline 127.0.0.1:64444: progress reported  done=1 total=1
pqscan: progress: 1/1 targets scanned
127.0.0.1:64444 group=- class=- suite=- version=- cert=-/- error=dial tcp 127.0.0.1:64444: connect: connection refused
  21:43:45.776 [info][output] emit 127.0.0.1: record emitted  format=text
── pqscan diagnostics ── schema 1 ── 0.0.1 (go1.27.2, darwin/arm64)
run: 2026-10-20T21:43:45.775767+11:00 → 2026-10-20T21:43:45.776132+11:00
flags: debug=true u=127.0.0.1:64444
events (5):
  21:43:45.775 [info][config] run : diagnostics armed  positional_args= version=0.0.1
  21:43:45.775 [info][engine] pipeline : multi-target scan started  max_window=1 progress_every=50 rate=0 total=1
  21:43:45.776 [error][tls] scan 127.0.0.1: TCP probe refused (dial tcp 127.0.0.1:64444: connect: connection refused)
  21:43:45.776 [info][engine] pipeline 127.0.0.1:64444: progress reported  done=1 total=1
  21:43:45.776 [info][output] emit 127.0.0.1: record emitted  format=text
summary: 5 events (1 errors, 0 warnings)
```

**Discussion.** Every decision point emits an event: plan steps, QUIC
handshakes, refusal classifications, timeouts, rate and breaker
decisions, WAL writes, emissions. The `[level][domain]` prefix is the
taxonomy: `[error][tls]` vs `[warn][quic]` vs `[info][engine]`. The
trailer block restates the run's shape (flags, window, totals). A
pasted stderr then reads self-describing.

### Attaching the machine-readable fault: -debug-out

**Problem.** A ticket needs the structured event log, not a paste.
Downstream tooling wants to query by domain, level and target.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u hostile.internal -quic-off -debug -debug-out diag.json
jq -c '.summary' diag.json
jq -r '.events[] | "\(.level)[\(.domain)] \(.op) \(.target // "-")"' diag.json
```

**Observation.** (live)

```json
{"events":5,"errors":1,"warnings":0}
```

```text
info[config] run -
info[engine] pipeline -
error[tls] scan hostile.internal
info[engine] pipeline hostile.internal
info[output] emit hostile.internal
```

**Discussion.** `-debug-out` writes the full event log as JSONL beside
the run. The log is independent of `-debug`'s stderr stream. Arm one
writer. Arm both at once. The event objects carry level, domain, op,
target, error and timing. The live view renders the same stream.
BUG REPORTS AND SCAN-TOUCHING FEATURE REQUESTS attach
`-debug -debug-out diag.json` output. The issue templates demand that
attachment. The event log is the only reproduction that shows the
tool's decisions.

### The failure taxonomy: reading scan results correctly

**Problem.** A red error line is not always a failure. A refused OFFER
is a finding. A timeout is an infrastructure problem. A breaker is the
tool protecting itself. Triage needs the classes.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l estate.txt -jsonl \
  | jq -r 'select(.error != "") | "\(.target.host): \(.error)"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

**Observation.** The classes and their meanings:

| class | reads as | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| refused (dial) | `connect: connection refused`, `no route to host` | nothing listening; the target is wrong or down |
| timeout / deadline | `i/o timeout`, `context deadline exceeded` | the deadline ladder (connect 2 s / handshake 4 s / probe 8 s, ±20 % jitter) fired — throttled or silently dropping |
| rejected (server) | `alert 40`, `tls: handshake failure`, `tls: bad certificate` | the server ANSWERED and said no — a finding, not a fault |
| refused (local) | `not-offerable locally: …` | pqscan cannot construct the offer — a tool capability boundary, stated in the record |
| breaker open | `breaker open` | the host's own failure budget tripped; no dial attempted for subsequent targets |

**Discussion.** Only the first two classes read "the target set is
unreachable". The `rejected` rows are ANSWERS. They feed the deep
modes' findings and the rubric. The local `refused` class should stay
zero for every supported codepoint. The release regression tests keep
it at zero. The breaker row is the congestion plane doing its job —
see the hostile-hosts recipe. The exit code stays zero for completed
scans. Per-target error records do not move it. A non-zero exit means
the RUN itself failed (binary fault, WAL unwritable, flag misuse).

### Hostile or flaky targets: rate, window, breakers

**Problem.** Dead subnets must not stall the run. A struggling host
must not take extra probe load.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l estate.txt -rate 2000 -threads 64 -jsonl
```

**Observation.** (live, `-rate 5` on 3 closed local ports — `time`
shows the bucket's launch-cadence floor; the same run uncapped for
contrast)

```text
real    0m0.412s        pqscan -l t3.txt -rate 5   (3 launches ≥ 0.4s at 5 rps: the bucket's floor)
real    0m0.019s        pqscan -l t3.txt           (uncapped)
```

**Discussion.** `-rate` meters launches through a token bucket.
`-threads` sets the in-flight cap. AIMD owns the window: grow on
successes, halve on probe timeouts, floor at one. A host that fails
consecutively trips ITS breaker. Later targets on that host emit
`breaker open` error records WITHOUT a dial (the taxonomy table's
row). The cooldown keeps the breaker open. Then it half-opens on a
single probe and closes on success. The defaults are
unbounded-sequential. The flags shape the run for the target list.

### Crash-resume and the WAL journal

**Problem.** A long run dies at 80 %. Do not pay for 80 % of the
handshakes twice. Do not lose the completed set.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l estate.txt -o out.jsonl          # interrupted mid-run
pqscan -l estate.txt -o out.jsonl -resume  # scans only the remainder
```

**Observation.** (live)

```text
pqscan: resume: WAL out.wal: 1 of 3 targets already complete; scanning 2
pqscan: progress: 2/2 targets scanned
```

**Discussion.** The WAL is an append-only journal beside the output
file. Every completed target lands there fsync-batched, under a
monotone sequence and a run id. A SIGKILL loses nothing but the socket
in flight. The output may run short. The journal does not. A resume
replays completed targets into the output (records ride through
unchanged). It probes only the difference. A run restarted with a
different target list composes: the journal's keys are `host:port`,
deduped in input order. The SLO: CI measures a 50-target run at ≤ 6 s
wall for the half.

## Records, output and triage

### The record and its consumers

**Problem.** A scan's value is downstream readability: triage, diffs,
machine consumption. The consumers need no bespoke parser.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l estate.txt -jsonl -o estate.jsonl        # streaming records
pqscan -l estate.txt -csv  -o estate.csv           # spreadsheet-shaped
pqscan -l estate.txt -urls | nuclei -silent -tags tls   # URL re-emission
```

**Observation.** The CSV contract is the record's flat form: 25
columns with the header on the first line:

```text
target,host,port,ptr,sni,negotiated,group_name,group_class,suite,version,alpn,quic_state,quic_group,udp_blocked,cert_sig_alg,cert_sig_pq,cert_key_alg,cert_key_pq,cert_dual,pq_score,pq_label,pq_hndl,pq_summary,error,ts
google.com,google.com,443,,,4588,X25519MLKEM768,pq_hybrid,TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256,tls-1.3,h2,negotiated,X25519MLKEM768,false,ecdsa-with-SHA256,false,ECDSA,false,false,40,pq-partial,false,negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40),,2026-10-20T10:25:32.034802Z
```

**Discussion.** The writers are hand-rolled. No reflection runs. No
`encoding/json` sits on the hot path. The goldens in the test tree pin
the column order in the CSV and the key order in the JSONL. A contract
change shows as a visible golden diff in review. A silent serde behavior
change cannot hide. The default output is the text one-liner for eyes.
`-jsonl` is the machine form. `-csv` is the archival form. `-urls` is
the re-emission for URL-taking scanners.

### The PQ rating view

**Problem.** A target list's post-quantum readiness needs a one-line
triage: where is the migration stuck? What must move first?

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l estate.txt -jsonl \
  | jq -c '{target:.target.host, group:.handshake.group_name, class:.handshake.group_class, score:.pq.score, label:.pq.label, hndl:.pq.hndl}'
```

**Observation.** One compact object per target (live. `-o` sends the
records to the file instead of the pipe. The triage jq reads stdout
directly):

```json
{"target":"google.com","group":"X25519MLKEM768","class":"pq_hybrid","score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false}
{"target":"example.org","group":"X25519MLKEM768","class":"pq_hybrid","score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false}
```

**Discussion.** The record scores itself. `pq.score` is the weighted
rubric sum. `pq.label` carries the band (`pq-ready` ≥ 80,
`pq-ready-hybrid` ≥ 60, `pq-partial` ≥ 40, `pq-missing` ≥ 1).
`pq.hndl` is the harvest-now-decrypt-later flag. It goes true when an
obsolete draft group accepts the handshake. Material intercepted
against such a handshake decrypts when the draft breaks. Escalate on
`hndl`. Treat the sub-60 bands as the worklist. The rubric feeds on the
negotiated-plane facts today. The certificate signature analytics ride
the `cert` block. `pq.score` rises through the same field as the deep
findings wire in.

### The rating in words: -explain

**Problem.** The text line's key=value fields are dense. A ticket or a
handoff needs the record read in sentences: what the rating means,
which layer is the gap. When nothing negotiated, the sentences also
read the error class.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -explain
```

**Observation.** (live) Under each text line, one reading block:

```text
google.com:443 group=X25519MLKEM768 class=pq_hybrid suite=TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 version=tls-1.3 alpn=h2 quic_neg=X25519MLKEM768 quic_class=pq_hybrid cert=ecdsa-with-SHA256/ECDSA pq=pq-partial(40)
  - rating: pq-partial 40/100. The negotiated key exchange is post-quantum. The certificate layer is classical. The lines below carry the detail.
  - key exchange: X25519MLKEM768 (pq_hybrid) — post-quantum hybrid: ML-KEM-768 + X25519. This group protects the session traffic. The harvest-now-decrypt-later risk does not apply while this group negotiates.
  - certificate: classical identity (ECDSA key, ecdsa-with-SHA256 signature). Use a PQ-signed or dual certificate at the next renewal.
  - quic: X25519MLKEM768 (pq_hybrid) on the UDP plane — the same post-quantum rating applies to h3 traffic.
```

Deep and pq runs add the plan reading. On `-mode deep` the executed
plan reads in operator words: the probe roll-up, the offered-one
matrix, the accepted rows (live, `pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -explain`):

```text
  - deep: the executed standard plan ran 24 probes: 3 accepted, 9 refused with the server's reasons, 12 not-offerable; the offered-one matrix read: group offer set 1/10, quic offer set 1/7, sigalg offer set 0/3, resumption vectors 0/3, hrr probe 1/1; accepted: group/29; quic/h3-exchange; hrr/x25519-shareless — the per-probe detail lives in the jsonl findings.
```

On `-mode pq` the reading names the accepted rungs and treats the
refusal mass as the expected default:

```text
  - deep: the forced PQ offer set sent 8 offers: 1 accepted, 7 refused with the server's reasons, 0 not-offerable; accepted: group/4588; each forced PQ-only group refused unless the server supports that group — the per-probe detail lives in the jsonl findings.
```

and a refused dial gets the error-class hint (the record's
zero-populated probe blocks read as the never-ran lines):

```text
  - quic: the lane never ran on this record.
  - error: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:65000: connect: connection refused — the probe reached no handshake. The endpoint is unreachable on this port (closed or filtered). No rating is possible.
```

**Discussion.** `-explain` is a `-text`-only selector. The machine
formats refuse it (exit 64, `pqscan: -explain applies to text output
only (drop the -jsonl selector)`). Every tail the text line carries
(`cert=sig/key`, the `deep=` counts, `ptr=`/`sni=` enrichment) has its
counterpart in the reading. The human format tells the same story the
machine formats carry.

### Self-explanation: -version and the completion scripts

**Problem.** Support and scripting need the tool's own identity. They
also need shell integration. The generators write them. Hand-maintained
flag lists do not.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -version
source <(pqscan -completion bash)     # zsh: pqscan -completion zsh > .../site-functions/_pqscan
```

**Observation.** (live) Source builds print the bare stamp. The
completion registers under the tool's name in bash:

```text
pqscan 0.0.1
```

```text
complete -F _pqscan_completions pqscan
```

**Discussion.** The scripts generate from the same flag surface the
`-h` help renders. The surface: every implemented flag, the
`-mode`/`-deep` `-sni`/`-completion` value lists, file completion where
a flag takes a path, plus BOTH dash spellings (`--word` parses anywhere
`-word` does).
The completions offer both spellings. Install one-liners and the
persisted locations live in INSTALL.md. Re-run the generator after an
upgrade. The completion then matches the binary. The `-version` stamp
is the release stamp on packaged builds.

## Downstream

### Feed nuclei

**Problem.** Give payload scanning to the tool that reads payloads.
Keep the handshake facts on this plane.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l assets.txt -urls | nuclei -silent -tags tls
```

**Observation.** `-urls` emits `scheme://host:port` per target: the
URL list any URL-taking scanner needs. The handshake/certificate/PQ
facts stay in pqscan's record stream (the `-o` file of the same run).

**Discussion.** The pipeline's stages compose by contract. Records
stream in input order. The WAL rests beside them. Each consumer reads
independently. The reverse also holds: masscan/naabu's output feeds
IN. nuclei's output feeds OUT. pqscan never inspects payloads.

### The PQ calendar

**Problem.** Readiness is a trajectory, not a snapshot. The reader
needs the week-over-week delta, not the raw JSON mass.

**Solution.**

```bash
# nightly, cron'd; the same target list, deterministic input order
pqscan -l estate.txt -csv -o /var/pqscan/$(date +%F).csv
diff /var/pqscan/yesterday.csv /var/pqscan/today.csv > /var/pqscan/pq-movement.diff
```

**Observation.** Repeat runs against a fixed list are comparable.
Input order and first-occurrence dedupe keep the stream deterministic.
The `ts` column orders the movement.

**Discussion.** Keep the diffs, not the runs. A day's movement is a
handful of rows: who moved up a band, who regressed, whose `hndl`
still fires. A CI job on the same contract gates merges in the target
set's own repos. A band-demotion PR surfaces there as a failing parity
check.

### Reverse-DNS workflow — IP ranges in, domains out

**Problem.** An IP sweep loses the SNI a domain run carries.
Certificate analytics without hostname context lose meaning on shared
infrastructure.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u 8.8.8.8:443 -ptr -sni auto -certs-dir certs/ -jsonl
```

**Observation.** The literal resolves pre-probe. The record carries the
answer verbatim. The PTR-derived candidate becomes the SNI. The
record's `ptr` and `sni_used` both fill. The PEM export leaves the leaf
for downstream tools:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"8.8.8.8:443","host":"8.8.8.8","ip":"","port":443,"ptr":"dns.google","sni_used":"dns.google"},"handshake":{"negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":true,"state":"negotiated","negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":true,"h3_direct":true}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"ecdsa-with-SHA256","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"ECDSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false,"summary":"negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40)"},"error":""}
```

**Discussion.** `-ptr` builds the run's pool off the system resolver
(bounded: 4 workers, a 2s budget, a 1024-entry LRU of positives).
Misses never cache. `-sni` sets the candidate rule: `auto`/`ptr-then-ip`
prefer the PTR name and fall back to the literal. `ip-only` always
takes the literal. The record's `sni_used` carries the candidate
actually used. `-certs-dir` writes the scan's end-entity certificate
per host (`<dir>/<host>.pem`). The scan then feeds a CA/policy pass
without a re-dial. A literal whose PTR does not resolve scans on the
literal. The miss records as an empty `ptr`. Enrichment is never a
blocker. Bulk PTR enumeration at scale stays with massdns or zdns.
Pre-filter there; hand the FQDNs forward.

## The flag map (live, landing, planned)

| Recipe topic | Flags / mode | State |
|---|---|---|
| one handshake, both planes | -u, -l and -l - (the stdin-file alias), the implicit piped stdin, -- (the bare marker), -jsonl or -json, -csv, -urls, -o, -resume, -quic-always, -quic-off, -debug, -debug-out | live |
| deep modes | -mode deep with -deep standard\|full | live |
| forced PQ ladder | -mode pq | live |
| the verdict in words | -explain (under -text; the machine formats refuse it) | live |
| self-explanation | -version, -completion bash\|zsh | live |
| rate/window/breakers | -rate, -threads | live |
| import adapters | -from-httpx, -from-naabu, -from-nuclei (one pinned capture command each, version-stamped in the recipes) | live |
| sharding | -shard i/n | live |
| identity hooks | -ptr, -sni, -certs-dir | live |
| port selection | -p | planned |
| profile config | -config, PQSCAN_* env | planned |
| legacy module | -legacy heartbleed,ccs,robot | planned |
| probe overrides | -probe-suite, -probe-group, -probe-sigalgs, -probe-version | planned |
| TLS fingerprints | -client-fingerprint, -jarm | planned |
| sort/fields/silent/stats | -sorted, -fields, -silent, -stats | planned |
| dial budgets | -timeout, -connect-timeout, -retries | planned |
| scale ceilings | -c, -dns-threads | planned |
| the HTTP probe | -http | planned |
| CIDR expansion | -cidr and CIDR spec lines (per-address expansion is not supported; tracked for follow-up) | planned |

The usage-drift gate in CI keeps USAGE.md and this map honest: a flag
without a man-page row fails the PR. A row outside the
implemented+planned set fails the PR. The flag map is where a new
operator starts.
